title: Is this a valid fear, or am I being unrealistic?

commenti.body: All of this is no reason to not go forth and pursue your stories like every other filmmaker in history. I don’t know if Hollywood ‘hates’ Iran necessarily but I’m sure the depiction of Iran in general is horribly skewed and as an Iranian you’re the best person to make that judgment. Again though, it’s not a reason to be discouraged. You have a point of view which is a powerful thing to have, so pursue your passion.

Most of Western culture?

If I were you, I would pay attention to how often I make sweeping generalisations. I would then think about how those generalisations impact and form my opinions.

Life has nuances. Art had nuances. People have nuances. Fucking find them and explore them.

I phrased it incorrectly so that's my bad. 

I'm sure a large number of groups, communities, and individuals in western culture are not like that. 

But it's hard to deny that western media and popular art has consistently perpetuating that narrative, and I doubt you could provide many examples that suggest otherwise. Also, in all fairness, considering the fact that large scale filmmaking is business-orientated, it makes sense from that standpoint why this is the case, it just isn't really something that would make money on a large-scale. I understand and accept that.

The one thing people would want to see is a depiction of your country through the eyes of their own home-grown artists. It could be gritty and realistic, or artful and stylized, but the key thing--and this holds true for any medium--is that it comes off as true. It's the same with any work of art you admire and love. Something about it feels so genuine and true (regardless of the style or how it's represented) that you can't help but open yourself up to it.

As another Middle Eastern guy, the last thing I want to see is depictions of privileged middle eastern men in very positive light. Sorry to break it to you, but most middle eastern countries have a long way to go in terms economic growth and human rights and I say this as someone who’s very critical of the west and Hollywood’s ignorant portrayal of us.

However, I think you can absolutely show the beauty of a country’s culture and its people in the form of an anthropological documentary, even if it’s about North Korea or Afghanistan, and people all over the world can still appreciate it if it’s well-executed.

When I think of Iranian film, I immediately think of A Girl Walks Home Alone At Night, and Persepolis.

Imagine, if at 16, Ana Lily Amirpour and Marjane Satrapi gave up their dreams of sharing their stories with the world, and telling their truth.

Becoming a filmmaker and becoming successful in the Hollywood machine are two different things. If your passion is to make films, then make films. It may not be easy, but making art never is.

Yeah, great point, it's great to shed light and be realistic about what those countries are like. On a more personal level though, I think it would be pretty cool to see a film where Middle Eastern characters, while not being privileged, are still not entirely defined by their issues. I feel like it's a fine line to walk between not ignoring the presence of the issues, while not making all Middle Easterns personality-less subhumans who only experience trauma, and nothing else. 

I feel like people would actually be more sympathetic towards those issues if the media they watched showed that Middle Easterns are still multi-faceted individuals with a variety of emotions.
[removed]

In a similar vein, you should not disregard the inherent imperialism rife in Western popular culture.

The white hegemony of Europe and the US consistently frames stories about or set outside of the West with white saviour tropes and an othering of the culture, values and people outside of their own.

OP didn't say that all the people he meets are prone to this, but the culture they live in and ingest certainly doesn't help and is definitely still pursuing stories that belittle, degrade and undermine those differences rather than embracing, exploring and opening the hearts and minds of audiences.

We live in a (Western) world where people review bombed a Marvel movie for having a female protagonist headline regardless of the quality because this was in advance of the release.

We live in a (Western) world where non-white heroes in mainstream tentpoles are still a rarity.

Check your privilege and don't shout at others for their legit experiences of white art being non-inclusive.

You don't need to apologise. Please don't apologise.

Your experience is genuine and your assessment is true.

The person replying to you is taking your valid assessment as a personal attack, exposing their embarassing fragilities and steadfast refusal to accept that the West are just as shameful in their portrayal of non-white culture as they have always been.

It's embarrassing. That person needs to do better and be respectful of the genuine experiences of cultures and peoples outside of his own bubble.

It isn't always easy, but that doesn't mean they shouldn't try.

You be you, OP xx

That's a really weird concern imho. It's not like the Hollywood and the west dictate the trade of moviemaking. For better or for worse, the entire modern world works under capitalism, and anyone can make movies as long as they acquire the backing of investors (the artistic merit of the result is another question entirely). And the last time I check capital investments also exist outside of the west.

> unfortunately, their films only ever get traction (at festivals) when they're playing the victim card (poverty, women's abuse, uncivilized), because if there's one thing that America hates, it's seeing a prosperous or happy Middle Eastern

I think you should watch more Iranian films. Iranian New Wave is definitely not about poverty porn. Most of the films of Makhmalbaf or Kiarostami for instance are intelligent looks at the role of cinema in society.

Wow. How insufferable you must be to infer and assume so much about me from one curt comment.

What do you know about my bubble or my respect of the genuine experiences of cultures and people outside of my bubble? Have we met before?

Would you agree that broad, basic statements about "the west" help us unpack the incredibly complex issue of race and representation in cinema? 

Is a generalisation saying that Americans hate seeing prosperous middle Eastern people a) accurate or b) helpful?

Can you also please point out where in my message I made a "steadfast refusal" to accept the west are shameful in their portrayals? "The west" is shameful.
And it's the most basic, unhelpful observation one can make. And I'm not going to give a sixteen year old a pat on the back for connecting those dots. 

I'm not American by the way, but you probably already knew that.

Back to OP.

My apologies, if my message came across dismissively, but your painting with very broad and unhelpful strokes.

1. Cinema is art - not content.
2. Nobody is owed art.

Is Hollywood a paragon? No. Has it ever been a paragon? No. So, why would you look for the perfect in the imperfect? Furthermore, why would you allow *that* to smother your passion? Please, please don't let that happen.

Will Hollywood ever be a paragon? Who knows, but OP, just because the cheese smells bad doesn't mean it's inedible. What does the state of Hollywood have to do with YOU telling the stories you think matter? If you want to make films that show a better vision of Iranians, then do. Don't use your generalisations as an excuse not to follow your passion - marginalised voices are more important than ever. Find the fuel for your art and set it ablaze, mate.
Let’s poll the Iranians to see what they think of women’s empowerment. On second thought, maybe not.

Can we also remember that OP is 16? Teens may ve prone to unnuanced opinions. That does not make them wrong. 

OP should pursue his dream, and who knows, he may teach the world something it needed to.

Absolute fucking drivel.

Let's poll Americans to see how many of them would still vote for Trump, shoot children who absent-mindedly wander onto their front lawns, and openly admit to not trusting people who aren't white.
[removed]

Wait, I thought your point was supposed to be this:

>If I were you, I would pay attention to how often I make sweeping generalisations. I would then think about how those generalisations impact and form my opinions.

...now you got me lost.

I don't know about film festivals and popular audiences, but my impression is that there are quite a few critically acclaimed Iranian films that don't portray people inherently as victims or barbarians. Have you seen "Close-up" by Kiarostami or "Children of Heaven"? These are very human stories that deal with issues that could be found anywhere, but yet are noticeably Iranian. I don't think the characters are barbarians or victims.

On the other hand, I think you're probably right when you suggest stories of Darius or Cyrus are not going to get much traction. The type of Westerners who watch non-Western films are also usually the type of people who prefer nuance and non-populist narratives rather than something simple and heroic - in other words people who don't watch pro-Greek/Western propaganda much either. If all you want to do is make an Iran-centric narrative that glorifies Darius or Cyrus, that's probably not going to fly in the West. Even so, there's a chance. The success of the rather nationalistic "RRR" from India with Western audiences shows that there is some space for that type of thing now. But I'd rather watch Kiarostami and such Iranian filmmakers, personally.

I do feel that there is a tendency in the West to prefer films from some places that problematizes life there in a way Western films don't need to promlematize Western realities. But I think Iran has been lucky enough not to fall prey to that as much as has my own country, South Africa. It is unfortunate that the films that get budgets and Western attention from here (think "Tsotsi") are generally much as you described.
My man that’s not even my comment.

Iran is consistently ranked as one of the most sexist and oppressively patriarchal countries in the world.

The United States, like most countries, trounces it in any criteria related to gender equality. The U.S. also generally ranks better in terms of racism, as well as general human rights.
My bad.  Dude looks like your twin though!

So that therefore legitimises Western art and creators to tar all Middle Eastern representation with the same brush?

What an abhorrent argument and perspective of the people that make up the world.
I am not sure where you got the idea that’s what I’m saying.
